item.description:

October 28, 202612:10 PM ET
By
The Associated Press
Dolores Huerta is seen at the California Democratic Party's 2025 State Convention at the Anaheim Convention Center in Anaheim, May 31, 2025.
Court Mast/AP
hide caption
toggle caption i
Court Mast/AP
Dolores Huerta, who co-founded the United Farm Workers union to improve working conditions in the nation's fruit and vegetable fields and coined the phrase "Sí, se puede!" that became a widespread rallying cry, has died. She was 96.
Huerta's family said in a statement through her foundation that she died Wednesday at home.
She kept a busy schedule well into her 90s, marching in protests and speaking in cities across the country about race, poverty, LGBTQ+ and women's rights on behalf of her Bakersfield, California-based foundation.
Huerta's resolve cemented her place in history as one of the nation's most influential labor leaders, civil rights icons and feminist activists. Her three-word Spanish-language slogan — which translates to "Yes, it can be done" — was grounded in the belief that people could affect change.

item.description:
What's gone up even faster than gas or rent? The cost of caregiving
October 28, 20269:05 AM ET
By
Kat McGowan
Cookie Jones, left, quit her job to provide care to her mother who has Alzheimer's disease. Caregivers often earn less as they take time off work to help aging family members.
Tyler Russell/Connecticut Public via Getty Images
hide caption

Tyler Russell/Connecticut Public via Getty Images
As prices have ticked up in recent years, the cost to caregivers has skyrocketed. A study, released Wednesday by AARP and shared first with NPR, finds that family caregivers — people helping out disabled, chronically ill or elderly adults — now spend an average $11,508 out of pocket each year. That's roughly 60% more than just five years ago, and adds up to 31% of a caregiver's income, on average.

item.title: Dozens are dead in a high-speed train crash in Spain
item.description:
Europe
Dozens are dead in a high-speed train crash in Spain
Updated October 28, 202612:02 PM ET
Originally published October 28, 20266:09 AM ET
By
The Associated Press
Emergency services attend to the victims at the scene of a collision between two trains in Urda, Spain, on Wednesday.
Juanma Jiménez/Europa Press via AP
hide caption
toggle caption i
Juanma Jiménez/Europa Press via AP
URDA, Spain — One high-speed Spanish train slammed into another that had stopped on the tracks Wednesday, killing at least 68 people and shredding carriages in the country's second deadly rail collision this year.
The regional government for Castilla La Mancha confirmed the death toll and said another 58 people needed medical treatment in hospital. Rescue workers continue to search in the wreckage for survivors and bodies.
The accident comes with memories still fresh of another crash between high-speed trains in southern Spain in January involving trains from the same two companies.
Spain's rail system operator ADIF said the crash occurred Wednesday morning in the province of Toledo, involving two high-speed trains carrying hundreds of passengers and heading in the same direction from the capital Madrid to Seville in southwestern Spain....

In key U.S. Senate races this year, candidates are soliciting donations from outside of their home states, and their out-of-state messaging is different from what they're running locally.
An NPR analysis of Google Ads for four major Senate races — Iowa, Georgia, Ohio and Texas — found that the Democratic and Republican candidates spent more than $15 million on advertising related to fundraising in the 2025-26 election cycle. About three quarters of that went to ads that ran nationally.

Jon Ossoff and Iowa Democratic nominee Josh Turek, more than 80% of their itemized individual contributions have come from out of state.

item.title: Why many student voters have a right to choose where to register to vote
item.description:
Explainer
Voting
Why many student voters have a right to choose where to register to vote
October 28, 20265:00 AM ET
Hansi Lo Wang
Students at the University of Virginia help eligible voters register to vote in Charlottesville, Va., in 2024.
Ryan M. Kelly/AP
hide caption
toggle caption i
Ryan M. Kelly/AP
Many student voters studying outside their hometown face a key decision before they even get a ballot: Should they register to vote where they go to school?
A Supreme Court ruling in 1979 affirmed the right of eligible students to register in the communities where they live during the academic year. But close to a half-century later, some people continue to question why students can vote in their college towns.
That issue resurfaced in discussions about changes Montana made last year to its requirements for residents who want to register to vote. After a student advocacy group sued, a state judge blocked the new restriction for now. That leaves the previous rules in place for Montana students who want to register to vote, including for the midterm elections through Election Day.
